questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Respiratory & vaccine-preventable disease epidemiology (measles, diphtheria, polio)
questions.stem: India was certified polio-free in:
options: 2014, after three years with no wild poliovirus case
questions.concept: The last wild case was in West Bengal in January 2011. Surveillance continues through acute flaccid paralysis reporting in all children under 15 and environmental sewage sampling.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Respiratory & vaccine-preventable disease epidemiology (measles, diphtheria, polio)
questions.stem: The secondary attack rate of measles is high because:
options: It is one of the most infectious diseases, with a basic reproduction number of 12 to 18
questions.concept: This high transmissibility means about 95% immunisation coverage is needed for herd immunity, far above the threshold for most other vaccine-preventable diseases.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Respiratory & vaccine-preventable disease epidemiology (measles, diphtheria, polio)
questions.stem: A case of measles is infectious from:
options: Four days before to four days after the appearance of rash
questions.concept: Infectivity begins in the prodrome, so isolation after the rash appears is too late to prevent spread - a key reason measles propagates so efficiently in schools and hospitals.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Respiratory & vaccine-preventable disease epidemiology (measles, diphtheria, polio)
questions.stem: Diphtheria is prevented by:
options: Toxoid, which produces antitoxic rather than antibacterial immunity
questions.concept: Because immunity is antitoxic, vaccinated persons may still carry the organism, which is why treatment of cases requires antitoxin and antibiotics and contacts require prophylaxis and boosting.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Respiratory & vaccine-preventable disease epidemiology (measles, diphtheria, polio)
questions.stem: Herd immunity is not applicable to which vaccine-preventable disease?
options: Tetanus, because it is acquired from the environment rather than person to person
questions.concept: Clostridium tetani spores are ubiquitous in soil, so every individual must be individually immunised. This is why maternal immunisation is essential for preventing neonatal tetanus.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Respiratory & vaccine-preventable disease epidemiology (measles, diphtheria, polio)
questions.stem: The pulse polio immunisation strategy works by:
options: Simultaneously immunising all children under five in a very short period to interrupt transmission
questions.concept: Simultaneous administration floods the community with vaccine virus, outcompeting wild virus in the gut and interrupting circulation - a strategy dependent on the live oral vaccine.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Respiratory & vaccine-preventable disease epidemiology (measles, diphtheria, polio)
questions.stem: Chickenpox is infectious from:
options: One to two days before the rash until all lesions crust
questions.concept: The rash is centripetal, appearing in successive crops so that lesions of different stages coexist - pleomorphism, which distinguishes it from smallpox where lesions were centrifugal and monomorphic.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Respiratory & vaccine-preventable disease epidemiology (measles, diphtheria, polio)
questions.stem: Smallpox eradication succeeded because of all EXCEPT:
questions.concept: There was no subclinical or carrier state, so every infectious person was identifiable - the crucial feature enabling surveillance and containment through ring vaccination.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Respiratory & vaccine-preventable disease epidemiology (measles, diphtheria, polio)
questions.stem: The epidemiological triad concept of an epidemic curve with a single sharp peak suggests:
questions.concept: A propagated epidemic shows successive waves separated by the incubation period as person-to-person transmission occurs, whereas a point source shows all cases within one incubation period.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Respiratory & vaccine-preventable disease epidemiology (measles, diphtheria, polio)
questions.stem: Mumps vaccine is given in India as part of:
options: The MMR vaccine in the private sector, as the national schedule uses MR
questions.concept: The Universal Immunisation Programme provides measles-rubella vaccine, while MMR including mumps is available in the private sector - a common point of confusion in examinations.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: International health, WHO, SDGs & disaster management
questions.stem: The Sustainable Development Goal specifically addressing health is:
options: Goal 3 - Ensure healthy lives and promote well-being for all at all ages
questions.concept: The 17 SDGs adopted in 2015 for 2030 replaced the 8 Millennium Development Goals, and are broader and universal, applying to developed and developing countries alike.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: International health, WHO, SDGs & disaster management
questions.stem: The SDG target for maternal mortality ratio by 2030 is:
options: Less than 70 per 100,000 live births globally
questions.concept: The neonatal mortality target is 12 or fewer and under-five mortality 25 or fewer per 1000 live births. India achieved the SDG maternal target ahead of schedule in several states.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: International health, WHO, SDGs & disaster management
questions.stem: The World Health Organization is best described as:
options: A specialised agency of the United Nations directing international health work
questions.concept: Established in 1948 with headquarters in Geneva and six regional offices, India belongs to the South-East Asia Region with its office in New Delhi. The World Health Assembly is its governing body.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: International health, WHO, SDGs & disaster management
questions.stem: The International Health Regulations require member states to notify WHO of:
options: Any event that may constitute a public health emergency of international concern
Only plague, cholera and yellow fever
questions.concept: The 2005 revision moved from a fixed disease list to an all-hazards approach with a decision instrument, requiring core surveillance and response capacity at points of entry.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: International health, WHO, SDGs & disaster management
questions.stem: In disaster management, triage aims to:
options: Do the greatest good for the greatest number by prioritising the salvageable
Treat the most severely injured first regardless of prognosis
questions.concept: This inverts everyday clinical ethics: those with catastrophic unsurvivable injuries are given expectant care so resources go to those who can be saved - the essence of mass casualty triage.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: International health, WHO, SDGs & disaster management
questions.stem: In the START triage system, the red (immediate) category indicates:
options: Life-threatening injury that is treatable with immediate intervention
questions.concept: Green denotes walking wounded, yellow delayed, red immediate and black dead or expectant. Rapid reassessment is essential as casualties can deteriorate between categories.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: International health, WHO, SDGs & disaster management
questions.stem: The commonest cause of death in the immediate aftermath of an earthquake is:
questions.concept: Epidemics do not arise spontaneously from dead bodies - a persistent myth. Disease risk comes later from displacement, overcrowding and disruption of water and sanitation.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: International health, WHO, SDGs & disaster management
questions.stem: The greatest public health priority in a refugee camp is:
options: Safe water, sanitation, food, shelter and measles immunisation
questions.concept: Measles vaccination with vitamin A is a top priority because overcrowding and malnutrition make measles outbreaks devastating, historically a major cause of camp mortality.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: International health, WHO, SDGs & disaster management
questions.stem: Primary health care as defined at Alma-Ata rests on principles including:
options: Equitable distribution, community participation, intersectoral coordination and appropriate technology
questions.concept: The Astana Declaration of 2018 reaffirmed these principles, linking them to universal health coverage and the SDGs, and emphasising empowered people and communities.

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: International health, WHO, SDGs & disaster management
questions.stem: Universal health coverage means that:
options: All people receive needed quality health services without financial hardship
questions.concept: Its three dimensions are population covered, services included and proportion of costs met. Reducing catastrophic out-of-pocket expenditure, which is very high in India, is central to it.
